"And I hope that work can be done so that we can take it up. It does have support in the House."

Asked about Bush's memo, a State Department spokesman said: "We've had good discussions with the Indian government on this matter, the 123 agreement, as well as a number of other issues. And we're going to be providing quite a bit of information...to the US Congress. And there's going to be testimony during that process. I'll let that testimony and the information that we've provided the Congress speak for itself."

(with PTI)

Heading: Cabinet clears biofuel policy - Indian Express
Content:
All Shiv Sena MPs of the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha have decided to donate their one-month salaries for providing relief to the flood-hit in Bihar.

"It is a national issue and we are second to none when it comes to extending humanitarian aid to our fellow countrymen," Rajya Sabha member and executive editor of the Sena mouthpiece Saamana told The Indian Express. "Our position vis-à-vis Biharis in Maharashtra is contextual to the problem of a lack of employment avenues for the local population, but we have no ill will for people living in different parts of the country."

On the face of it, whatever Raut says may seem reasonable, but if seen in the backdrop of Raj Thackeray's latest attempts to tap Marathi sentiments at the cost of the Sena, it is a daring move.

Sources in the Sena said the party leadership was not unduly worried over the threat posed by Raj. They said the Sena was committed to social, cultural and political aspirations of the people of Maharashtra as well as Hindutva, but it was conscious of the fact that the events, which coincided with the birth of Maharashtra and also the Sena, could not be replayed. "No matter who incites Marathi passions, the Sena alone has the wherewithal to encash them during elections," they added.

Heading: Army chief briefs PM on Pak - Indian Express
Content:
In a bid to cut down on India's hefty fuel import bills, the Government has decided to increase the amount of biofuels that can be mixed with petrol and diesel, targeting a level of 20 per cent by 2017.

After a two-year-long debate, the Cabinet cleared the National Biofuel Policy on Thursday. Conscious that the decision was bound to reignite the debate over food vs fuel, the Government said it would encourage bio-diesel plantations on government or community wastelands and not on fertile soil. It said the focus would be on indigenous production of bio-diesel feedstock and import of free fatty acid such as oil or palm would not be permitted.

As of now, India allows ethanol to be mixed in petrol upto a maximum of five per cent of the total volume and there is talk of doubling this to 10 per cent by next year. Nearly 70 per cent of India's oil demand is met through imports.

The biofuel policy approved on Thursday stipulates that bio-diesel and bio-ethanol be brought under the ambit of 'declared goods' to ensure unrestricted movement of

bio-fuels within and outside the states. The Government will levy no taxes or duties on bio-diesel.

The Cabinet also approved the setting up of an empowered National Biofuel Coordination Committee headed by the Prime Minister and a Biofuel Steering Committee headed by Cabinet Secretary.

Heading: After wheat, Govt plans emergency rice reserves - Indian Express
Content:
With Pakistan's western frontier on the boil after a series of attacks on militant targets by US-led forces, Indian Army chief General Deepak Kapoor met Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to give him a brief on the security situation in the neighbouring country. Kapoor, who met Singh on Friday morning, is believed to have given an assessment of the situation along Pakistan's western borders and the impact it is likely have on India, especially on Kashmir.

The meeting, which has been termed as a review of 'security situation in view of developments in the neighbourhood', comes days after it came to light that US forces have been given authorisation by President Bush to strike within Pakistani territory.

The Indian Army has been keeping a close eye on developments on Pakistan's western border. Army analysts believe any developments there have a direct influence on the security situation along the Indo-Pak border.

Heading: Delhi: LJP to contest all seats - Indian Express
Content:
After having created three million tonnes of wheat emergency reserves, the Government is now planning to create two million tones of emergency rice reserves this year. This was informed by Agriculture and Food Minister Sharad Pawar at the 'Warehousing 2008' conference in the Capital on Friday. The announcement comes in the backdrop of an earlier directive from the PMO to create a strategic reserve for foodgrain to meet any emergency.

With the two million tones of emergency rice reserves on top of three million tones of wheat reserves, the country will have five million tonnes of emergency reserves of foodgrain. These reserves have been made possible because of the record procurement of wheat and rice this year. The government agencies have procured 225 lakh tonnes of wheat this year, which is more than double the procurement last year. As for rice, the procurement is over 274 lakh tonnes as compared to 249.66 lakh tonnes by this time last year.

Heading: Don’t make Tata agreement public: HC to Bengal - Indian Express
Content:
LJP chief Ramvilas Paswan on Friday announced candidates for all the 70 Assembly seats of Delhi, apparently to check the rise of BSP chief Mayawati.

Paswan, who is known for his animosity towards the BSP supreme, is learnt to have decided to contest all the Delhi Assembly seats. The move is likely to cut into Mayawati's Dalit votebank that would ultimately benefit the Congress.

Paswan, however, refuted the gameplan. He said that the decision had been taken much ahead in a bid to expand the party. Asked as to why he was not contesting in alliance with the Congress, Paswan said: "Being part of the UPA does not mean that everywhere I will have an alliance with the Congress. Even NDA allies go alone in many states."

The Mayawati-led BSP too is contesting all the Delhi Assembly seats and had declared the candidates earlier on. Treading the same path, Paswan released a list of his party candidates on Friday.

Heading: Minister Raja to push for extension of STP benefits - Indian Express
Content:
Justice Dipankar Dutta of the Calcutta High Court on Friday directed the West Bengal Government not to make public the ''secret'' part of the agreement between Tata Motors and the state Government for the next two weeks. On Friday, the counsel for Tata Motors moved a petition apprehending that the secret part of the agreement might be disclosed by the state Government as well as the West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation.

Advocate Samaraditya Pal, counsel for Tata Motors, moved a plea saying WBIDC had already published a portion of the agreement between the state Government and the company signed on March 9, 2007. He claimed the Government and the WBIDC violated legal provisions of the Right To Information (RTI) Act 2005 by disclosing the agreement.

WBIDC had disclosed the portion of the agreement in their website on September 5 after a directive from the Chief Information Commissioner of the state. The website disclosed the three-page agreement between the state Government and Tata Motors on September 5 even as discussions between the Government and the Trinamool Congress were continuing at the Raj Bhavan.

After Sudip Bandopadyay, Congress MLA and chairman of the Standing Committee on Business and Commerce, put pressure on the Government to make the agreement public, the Commerce and Industries Minster Nirupam Sen read out the portion of the agreement at a meeting of the committee on August 27.

Heading: ‘Cheaper crude is fine, but no fuel price cut’ - Indian Express
Content:
Union minister for IT and Communication A Raja today said he would appeal to the government to extend the tax concessions given to Software Technology Parks (STPs) for one more year.

As tax concessions given to STPs are expected to end in 2009, Raja said he would request Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and finance minister P Chidambaram to extend the rebates for one more year.

He was delivering the address at the inaugural session of the 'Connect 2008', a three-day seminar on 'Global Competitiveness and Equitable Growth — Driven by Innovation', organised by industry body CII here.

"In order to promote software exports, Department of Information Technology (DIT) has established Software Technology Parks under the STPI scheme. The unique feature of STPI is its transparent policy environment, single window clearance and a clutch of tax concessions," he said. "I can't assure you now, but I will try to speak with Prime Minister and Finance Minister for extending the scheme for one more year," he said.

Referring to the theme of the event, Raja said, "Industry needs sustained growth and it can be achieved only through constant innovation. However, it (innovation) should not be only for the advancement of technology but should also enable common man to gain more knowledge from it." The Centre's semi-conductor policy had helped get over Rs 1 lakh crore of foreign investments in the country, he said.

Raja said India's software and services exports were $40.3 billion in 2007-08 compared with $31.4 billion in 2006-07. "The IT-BPO industry employs about two million professionals, out of which 1.5 million are in the export segment," he said, adding indirect employment in this industry was about six to eight million. He stressed for developing infrastructure in Tier II and Tier III cities to accommodate the growing IT-ITes industry in new cities.

Heading: When all else fades out, VCs jumpcut to films - Indian Express
Content:
Petroleum minister Murli Deora today said there were no plans to cut fuel prices in immediate future, while terming the fall in global crude prices to the lowest in six months as a "welcome" change.

Crude prices are hovering near 100 dollars a barrel level after hitting a six-month low of 98 dollars yesterday. "I welcome this that crude prices have come down," Deora told reporters here, however, he added that the government was not considering any fuel price revision at the moment.

Petroleum secretary R S Pandey said that crude prices were expected to fall even further. "Over the last one and a half months, crude prices have come down from the peak of $147 per barrel. The Indian basket of crude reached an average $95.47 a barrel, which is a welcome relief. We expect prices to fall further, which would be a real relief," Pandey said.

"If crude stays at current levels for the entire financial year of 2008-09, the extent of under-recoveries is estimated at Rs 1,62,254 crore. But even this figure is very high," Pandey said.

According to June data, estimated under-recoveries of state-run oil firms Indian Oil Corp, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum stood at Rs 2,45,305 crore. If crude prices stayed at current levels, under-recoveries for the entire year were estimated to fall to Rs 1,62,254 crore, Pandey said.

Heading: Sahara group firm to exit NBFC biz - Indian Express
Content:
While talk of an economic slowdown is affecting the morale of the manufacturing industry, it is surely helping a set of funds. These funds are not only looking at providing the much-needed capital to creative personnel to launch a movie but are also looking at buying stake in established production houses. While two firms have firmed up plans, more such funds are in the pipeline.

Vistaar Religare Film Fund (VRFF), a Sebi-regulated venture capital (VC) film fund, which had closed its first tranche of fund raising in April has already announced to invest around Rs 78 crore to make 8 films. "The films have been budgeted between Rs 5 and Rs 20 crore and the first project is on the floor," said managing director of VRFF, Sheetal Talwar. The fund intends to have a corpus of Rs 200 crore. Another fund close on the heels of VRFF is Cinema Capital Venture Fund (CCVF). However, it has a different business model and will primarily focus on buying stake in content generating companies. CCVF has identified six-eight companies in which it would like to buy stakes. "We are in talks and in some cases they are in advanced stages. We plan to invest Rs 40-100 crore in these companies to buy 10-49 per cent stake in them," said founder managing director of CCVF Samir Gupta.

"Apart from identifying companies in which we would like to own stake, CCVF will also launch joint ventures and special purpose vehicles (SPVs) with production houses to invest in their projects. After the completion of the project the SPV would be wound up with proportionate distribution of the propfits between the fund and the production house," said Gupta. The fund is in its first phase of raising funds and plans to garner Rs 500 crore. "We may have around 3,000 investors in our fund when it closes on September 30 as the minimum ticket size investment is Rs 10 lakh," Gupta added. The fund will also look at providing seed capital to established actors, directors and writers who would like to set up their own company.

Since entertainment spends in recessionary periods historically show an upward trend, VC firms and private equity funds who wish to take part in the Indian media and entertainment sector growth story seem to be moving ahead with a lot of conviction, said an analyst. "The Indian media and entertainment (M&E) industry is poised to enter a golden era. One of the largest markets in the world, the industry is seeing strong growth and has the potential to garner $25 billion by 2012," says a PWC-Ficci industry report.

Heading: Dollar-weary tech firms lead Sensex rout - Indian Express
Content:
The Reserve Bank of India on Friday announced that Sahara India Investment Corporation Ltd (SIICL) has moved out from its non-banking financing business. "SIICL, which is one of the group companies belonging to the Sahara group, as such cannot transact the business of non-banking financial institutions," RBI said.

RBI said that the Subrata Roy-promoted SIICL has voluntarily exited the non-banking financial business and its certificate of registration has been cancelled as of August 11, 2008. "Sahara India Investment Corporation Ltd (a non-deposit taking non-banking finance company) has voluntarily surrendered the license to act as a NBFC. The management has decided to carry out real estate business in the said company.

"The above company is distinct from Sahara India Financial Corporation Ltd, which is a residuary non -banking company involved in the business of para banking that is deposit mobilisation," said a Sahara spokesperson. He said SIICL was a non-deposit taking company and had decided to quit the NBFC business to enter into the real-estate sector. Following litigation, the RBI had recently asked SIFCL not to accept new deposits that mature beyond June 30, 2011 and gradually reduce the aggregate liability to zero by June 30, 2015.

Heading: Industrial output surges to hit 7.1 per cent in July - Indian Express
Content:
The BSE Sensex fell 2.26 per cent on Friday to its lowest close since late July, led by losses in software outsourcers such as Infosys Technologies and Tata Consultancy Services on worries that the dollar's rise against the euro and pound could impact the export-driven firms' revenue growth. The rupee, which is tumbling to the 46 level, ended at 45.75/76 per dollar, 0.4 per cent weaker than its previous close. Infosys fell 6 per cent to its lowest close in a month, and Tata Consultancy lost 3.3 per cent. Satyam Computer Services closed 3.5 per cent lower and Wipro shed 1.7 per cent, with the export-driven companies finding little comfort in the rupee's fall to a two-year low against the dollar.

When Will the buck stop?

The rise of dollar against different currencies in the current quarter

Rupee 5.5 per cent

Pound 13.8 per cent

Euro 13 per cent

What's with the rupee?

The rupee fell to its lowest in nearly two years on Friday as offshore-related dollar demand and weak stocks hurt, while better-than-expected industrial output data failed to provide much respite. The partially convertible rupee ended at 45.75/76 per dollar, off a low of 45.80, its weakest since October 11, 2006 and 0.4 percent weaker than its close of 45.56/57 on Thursday. It has shed nearly 4 per cent in September, taking its losses in 2008 to 13.85 per cent.

Capital outflow gains currency

There is pressure on the rupee because of capital outflows and it is likely to continue to weaken unless the state-run banks decide to defend the rupee decisively as they are the only dollar sellers at the moment. Exporters were not selling very aggressively and offshore-related demand is also hurting the rupee

Infosys says...

Infosys Technologies' could see its dollar revenues hit by the rise of the US currency against euro and British pound, although the rupee's fall would lessen the impact, its chief financial officer said. But it was too early to speculate about the impact on the dollar revenue guidance of India's second-largest software services exporter, V. Balakrishnan told Reuters on Friday. "The impact on reported dollar numbers could be there ... because other currencies have weakened against the dollar, it could be a lesser dollar number," he said.

Wipro says...

Wipro Ltd, India's third-ranked software services exporter, does not see currency volatility having an impact on its September quarter earnings, a senior official said on Friday. "We don't rely on cross-currency volatility to drive our business," Suresh Vaswani, the joint chief executive of Wipro's IT business, said. "We have a strong and conservative hedging policy and we try to hedge our cross-currency movements using that." Vaswani said although the current business environment was challenging there were opportunities as well as companies look to cut costs.

Heading: RGPPL to provide extra 600 MW to Maharashtra - Indian Express
Content:
Industrial growth unexpectedly rebounded in July with the growth in the index of industrial production (IIP) touching 7.1 per cent. This is the second-highest growth level it has accomplished since February, when it was at 8.7 per cent. Annual IIP growth hit rock bottom earlier in March this year, when it fell to 3 per cent. The cumulative growth witnessed over the April-July period stands at 5.7 per cent over the corresponding period last year.

Data issued by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation showed that the index stood at 273, as against 252.2 last year. The figure is above market expectations of around 6 per cent amidst concerns of an imminent slowdown in industrial growth as a result of the tight monetary policy undertaken by the Reserve Bank of India.

The biggest drivers of this surprise spike were the capital goods and consumer durables industries, which grew by a healthy 21.9 per cent and 11.2 per cent respectively. Last year, capital goods production had risen by 12.9 per cent and production in consumer durables had fallen by 3.2 per cent. Analysts believe this rise could also partly be a base effect considering that the index had declined by about five points in July last year.

"As expected, consumption goods have shown strength, but the positive surprise was from capital goods," Yes Bank chief economist Shubhada Rao said.

Seven of the 17 industry groups which comprise the IIP basket, saw negative growth rates. These included food products, leather products, wood and wood products, rubber, plastic, petroleum and coal products, etc.

However, there is also concern that the effect of the monetary tightening measures undertaken by the central bank haven't played out yet and industrial growth could likely take a hit when it does begin to take effect. Moody's Economy.com said industrial production has shown mild fluctuation in recent months, but there is clearly a downward trend.

This, however, did not prevent the industry from celebrating the resurgence in growth. A release issued by Confederation of Indian Industry said, "IIP growth to 7.1 per cent in July as compared to 5.2 per cent growth during April-June '08 is quite encouraging... CII has observed that double-digit growth in both capital and consumer durable goods is a sign of healthy investment and consumer spending in the economy."

A statement by Assocham said, "Since inflation is coming down, industrial production will register positive growth. Although, it is not sure whether IIP expansion in 2008 will be as good as in the previous year."

(With Agencies)

Heading: In eye of credit storm, Lehman searches for survival options - Indian Express
Content:
In a relief to power deficit Maharashtra, the Ratnagiri Gas and Power Private Limited (RGPPL) project is expected to pump in an additional 600 MW into the state grid by the end of September, and also plans to generate power at full capacity by end of March 2009. The project is currently generating around 650 MW.

State energy minister Dilip Valse Patil on Thursday said officials from US-based General Electric (GE), which has supplied the 9 FA-class turbines, had assured that the problems with the project would be sorted out and hoped to generate an extra 600 MW by September-end.

After Patil expressed concern about the breakdowns, GE officials denied any defects in the turbines but agreed to maintenance and repair problems, which resulted in the generation shortfalls in the project.

Senior officials concerned with the exercise said GE had promised the RGPPL that it would operationalise another 300 MW by December-end by commissioning another unit. The plant is expected to run on full capacity by March-end after another 300 MW capacity comes on track, they added.

"This (additional 600 MW) will help ease out the situation as the load starts rising in October due to the rabi season, sugar factories beginning production and the festive season. GE is fairly optimistic as they have identified the problems," said the official.

He added that the major problem lay in the continuous failure of compressor blades. "It seems that GE and RGPPL have done some technical analysis and are doing the modification and repairs," the official said.

The state cabinet had recently approved the grant of Rs 300 crore loan guarantees to the RGPPL to seek a loan from the Power Finance Corp (PFC) to purchase spare parts for the repairs in the 2,150 MW project. The meeting of the RGPPL board on August 29 cleared the purchase and repairs orders to commission the units.

Patil also said he would be visiting New Delhi on Monday to attend a meeting of RGPPL and GE and would also meet also Union power minister Sushilkumar Shinde, minister of state for energy Jairam Ramesh and Union petroleum minister Murli Deora.

Heading: Commodities guru bullish on gold and crude - Indian Express
Content:
No corporate leader wants to be backed into a corner, but that's where Lehman Brothers' CEO Richard Fuld is now. He's right where he belongs. For months, Fuld, 62, thought the firm he has worked at since he left college could outrun the credit storm rather than deal with its consequences.

That misplaced bet is punishing Lehman now, leaving it teetering on the edge of collapse unless it can find a bank or other investment firm willing to rescue it. There is no denying that the current credit crisis is unprecedented. Financial institutions globally are facing huge write-downs and losses on their real-estate investments that went bad.

The problem is that Lehman's top brass kept thinking they knew better. Wait the housing and mortgage downturn out, they thought, and then conditions will improve and so will our business. That's why they were slow to mark down the value of their damaged assets to reflect current market conditions.

Back in April, Fuld said that the worst was "behind us" regarding the credit crisis. He ate those words weeks later.

Even after it was apparent that Lehman hadn't escaped the credit storm, its leadership never seemed to commit entirely to getting this mess under control. That's why so much attention went to Wednesday's announcement of a Lehman rescue plan. Fuld said the firm would explore all other options, including the sale of the entire company.

Even the rhetoric that Lehman's executives used didn't do much to settle the nerves of jittery investors. Lehman had its chance again to tell the marketplace it was on the case with a concrete plan — at least a named buyer for its investment management division. Lehman blew it. The stock resumed its freefall.

Lehman's leaders are now scrambling desperately to find a buyer. For the first time in this crisis, they seem to be moving fast.

Heading: UAE firm is willing to pump Rs 2K crore into Tripura - Indian Express
Content:
Despite the recent downturn in the major globally-traded commodity prices, Jim Rogers, commodity investment guru and chairman of Singapore-based Rogers Holdings, remains optimistic and bullish on crude oil and gold and also upbeat on select agri-commodities like sugar, cotton and coffee.

Crude oil prices have dropped 30 per cent to $100 a barrel on Friday, since reaching a record $147.27 a barrel on July 11, 2008. Gold prices have also declined 27 per cent to trade at $750 on Friday, from the current year's peak of $1023.50 an ounce on March 17, 2008.

Crude oil price will continue to rise, because there is a major demand-supply mismatch. "I am still bullish on crude oil and gold," he said.

"Crude oil will rise over the longer term as no major crude oil discovery has happened in the last 40 years. As far as gold is concerned, no new mines have recovered over the past decade and some mines are over 100 years old," Rogers said, on the sidelines of Commodity Equities Fund launched by Birla Sun Life on Friday.

Sugar and silver prices globally have corrected over 40 per cent in the recent days whereas gold prices have corrected over 25 per cent, he added.

"I am bullish on opportunities in the agricultural commodities market. I am investing there now like in sugar and cotton. The bull market in commodities will continue to go on now for some years," Rogers said. "Commodities are safe to invest as they do not require any governance, there are no disclosures required," he quipped in his inimitable style.

Agricultural stocks are at 60-year lows and as far as demand is concerned, income levels are rising in some Asian countries. Current hot picks in the agri-commodities are sugar, coffee, zinc, cotton and silver, he added.

"Farmers in India and the US are going to be extremely rich. The 29-year Maserati driving stock market executives will be driving tractors for 29-year-old farmers in the next decade," said the peripatetic Rogers, who also features in the Guinness Book of World Records for motorcycling for over 1,00,000 miles across six continents.

"I am going to try and buy little bit of gold here in India. If gold continues to go down, I am smart enough to buy more gold. Price could go to $525 an ounce and could have a big correction," he said.

"It is better to buy when commodities prices are going down rather than when they are going up but I have no idea whether this is the best time," he said.

About the future movement of US dollar, he said, "I am very pessimistic about the future movement of US dollar value." Dollar will continue to deteriorate over the next two decades as many oil producing countries (especially OPEC) have already started delinking of dollar.

US dollar is a terribly flawed currency and it has got terrible problems down the road, he added. He then reminded that a around less than a century ago the pound sterling was the standard global currency and now it had lost this prominent place.

Heading: RBI asks banks to activate no-frill accounts - Indian Express
Content:
The United Arab Emirates-based Techmate International has expressed it's interest in investing Rs 2,000 crore in Tripura and asked for 300 acres from the government for the purpose, official sources said.

A four member delegation of the industrial house led by Ansar Abdul Gafoor called on chief minister Manik Sarkar and industries minister Jiten Chowdhury last night and expressed their interest in setting up of an international medical city and a global village for IT industry as well as investments in tourism.

Sources said that if the government assured Techmate the 300 acres, the company would initiate the process by next November. Chowdhury said tech group consultant Shamrock Consultancy had earlier visited the state and made a survey on investment opportunity for Techmate.

Italy is also interested to invest in tripura, official sources said. The Italian consul general Bruno Camparia met Sarkar and Chowdhury yesterday to discuss the possibility of investment.

Heading: Sibling firms can’t vie for same deal? - Indian Express
Content:
With most no-frill accounts opened by customers in banks remaining non-operative, the Reserve Bank has asked the banks to offer credit products through no-frill accounts for rural and semi-urban customers and use the business correspondent model effectively to promote financial inclusion in areas where banking facilities are not available.

"We have laid the foundation for financial inclusion by opening more no-frill accounts in rural sectors. But many of these accounts remain non-operative. They (banks) should see it as a huge business opportunity and offer credit to customers," RBI deputy governor Usha Thorat said.

Though state-owned and private-sector banks have been successful in opening no-frill accounts in semi-urban and rural areas, many of these accounts remain inactive. No-frill accounts opened by commercial banks rose to 1,58,37,862 in 2008 so far, compared with 67,24,667 in 2007.

Heading: Great leap to the present - Indian Express
Content:
In what may set a precedence for companies with same parentage bidding for big-ticket infrastructure projects in India, the government has rejected the application of PSA International and Neptune Orient Lines, both owned by Temasek Holdings, a Singapore government-owned investment entity.

According to government sources, Ennore Port Ltd (EPL), which had issued a request for qualification (RFQ) for developing the Rs 1,300-crore mega-container terminal on a build-operate-transfer (BOT) basis, invoked the commonality-of-interest clause, as per the advice of the Planning Commission. PSA is fully-owned by Temasek and NOL, 68 per cent.

PSA has, however, contested the move stating that the two companies had distinct management structures and were not related in any other way.The Planning Commission, which is corresponding with SBI Caps, the consultant to the port public-private partnership project has, however, said the two were majority held by Temasek and hence did not qualify for the project.

The project is already mired in controversy with some big global operators not making it to the final shortlist because of poor scores. Besides PSA and NOL, Dubai's DP World, another big operator, too does not figure in the shortlist of six. The new 'model' RFQ norms for infrastructure projects specify that only six operators be short-listed. This itself has become an issue being challenged in court by some of the 22 consortia that put bids for the project.

Ennore Port had issued the tender inviting bids for the development of the 1,000-metre container terminal in April this year. However, soon after the final shortlist of developers was announced, four operators, including PSA dragged the government-run port authority to court questioning the basis on which the companies were short-listed and seeking a stay on the tendering process.

While no stay has been granted yet, the delay and uncertainty is likely to take a toll on many other port public-private partnership projects. For now, the shortlist has been sent to the Public Private Partnership Appraisal Committee (PPPAC) for approval. The other companies/consortia that filed writ petitions against Ennore Port include Sical Infra Assets Ltd, a member of the PSA-led consortium, ABG Infralogistics and the India Terminal consortium.

Heading: Line of no control - Indian Express
Content:
Except for India and China there are no two large neighbours whose relations over time have fluctuated so sharply as to rival the roller coaster. The kathakali act staged by China at the Nuclear Suppliers' Group meeting in Vienna only confirms this. The age of Hindi-Chini Bhai-Bhai was followed, after the brief but brutal border war in the high Himalayas in 1962, by an era of Hindi-Chini bye-bye. The relationship remained frozen for 14 years, despite Indira Gandhi's 1968 initiative to offer China "unconditional" talks, dropping the prior insistence on Chinese acceptance of the Colombo proposals aimed at narrowing the gap between the two sides' positions.

Mao Zedong responded positively on May Day in 1970, smiling at the Indian charge d'affaires, Brajesh Mishra. But the Bangladesh crisis unavoidably escalating into war put paid to the exercise. China, like the United States, was on the side that was morally in the wrong and militarily doomed to defeat. Some months earlier, Henry Kissinger's famous secret visit to Beijing had led to the dramatic US-China rapprochement. Given China's firm support to its "all-weather friend", Pakistan, New Delhi's response to the US-China-Pakistan line-up was to sign the Indo-Soviet treaty. This miffed the Chinese even more.

Yet, in 1976, Indira Gandhi took another initiative to break the ice with China. She sent K.R. Narayanan, later president of India, as ambassador to Beijing to end the practice since 1959 of each country's embassy in the other being headed by a charge. The next year she was out of power. But the Janata government, while rejecting much else she stood for, stuck to her policy of repairing the relationship with China. In 1979, the then foreign minister, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, went to Beijing. Whatever good this sojourn could have done was wiped out by the Chinese invasion of Vietnam, a good friend of India, while Atalji was still on Chinese soil.

Shortly after returning to power in 1980, at Joseph Broz Tito's funeral in Belgrade, Indira Gandhi met Mao's successor, Hua Guofeng, and the two agreed to resume the ruptured India-China dialogue. Due to begin October 1980, it was delayed by eight months because of Chinese pique over Indian recognition of the Vietnam-backed Heng Samrin government in Cambodia.

For a long time the dialogue remained excruciatingly slow and generally arid, because India gave primacy to the vexed boundary question on which the Chinese were not prepared to budge from their original stand. However, in P.V. Narasimha Rao's time, the two countries agreed to put the border issue on the back burner, to maintain peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), that has by and large prevailed, and to improve relations in other spheres.

Despite China's sharp reaction to the 1998 nuclear tests the dialogue was soon back on track, and by the turn of the century a spurt in economic and trade relations had begun that has since assumed phenomenal proportions. The phase of Hindi-Chini buy-buy had started. With the two-way trade reaching $40 billion, China is on the verge of becoming this country's largest trading partner though euphoria over this should be tempered by three factors.

First, Indian exports are largely of iron ore and other raw materials. Second, $40 billion, staggering in Indian eyes, is but a small proportion of China's trade surplus of over $200 billion with the US alone. Third, and most significant, the Chinese stand on the border question has become increasingly vehement, claiming the whole of Arunachal Pradesh, especially the Tawang tract. This runs counter to the agreement in principle between Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and his Chinese counterpart, Wen Jiabao, that, in negotiating the boundary, populated areas must not be disturbed. But Beijing does not care. Nor should it be overlooked that China has subtly done all it could to deny India a permanent seat on the UN Security Council, and even entry to the Asia-Europe summit and several other forums.

To complete the context of China's intriguing behaviour at Vienna, it must be added that China has taken due notice of Rising India and of the qualitative change in India-America relations but it still does not regard this country to be in the same league as it is in. This results in Beijing's dual policy of befriending this country up to a point and simultaneously containing it to the extent possible. A mixture of cooperation and competition is built into the pattern of relationship among all the major actors on the world stage. However, the element of conflict in the complex India-China equation is greater than in the bilateral relationship between such powers as the US, the European Union, Russia and Japan. The only difference is that China is cognisant of the ground reality and acts accordingly.

By contrast we try to live on hope, assumptions and even wishful thinking.

The goings-on over the NSG waiver fit into this pattern nicely. It is no secret that ever since the July 18, 2005 agreement was signed, China has tried discreetly and indirectly to either sabotage the Indo-US deal or to ensure that Pakistan, too, gets the same treatment. Whatever Chinese leaders might have said to their Indian interlocutors privately, China never said publicly that it "would not stand in the way" of the deal going through the NSG. From all accounts, China was convinced that the six dissenters in Vienna would dig their heels in and block the deal. Only when it realised that it had overestimated the determination of the "like-minded six" and underestimated the force of the American juggernaut, did China emerge from the shadows and show its hand. However, when all the six dissenters were on board, China also went along with the consensus.

Those who say that New Delhi should not have expressed its displeasure with China during the visit of Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi should spare a thought for the dismal fact that both President Hu Jintao and Premier Wen Jiabao declined to take the prime minister's calls. Which brings me to my main point: India must not adopt a confrontational attitude towards the northern neighbour, but it should not be as hesitant, gingerly and mealy-mouthed as it has usually been.

The writer is a Delhi-based political commentator

express@expressindia.com

Heading: Minimum city - Indian Express
Content:
The word "ally" is in danger of becoming another of those words in the English language that have been bent out of shape by modern politics. When word emerged from Washington of the Bush administration's decision to permit its special operations teams to operate inside Pakistan's troubled tribal areas — without the prior approval of the Pakistani government — reactions ranged from the approving to the outraged; but the most percipient of those recognised that real allies don't do that to each other. Notwithstanding American claims that the Pakistanis had agreed to the "general concept" and Pakistani claims that they had thought the idea was "still under discussion", it seems clear that something has fractured in that relationship: the Durand Line is not the only line that has been crossed.

America's frustration is understandable, especially to those in India who have known for years that Pakistan's margins encompass well-equipped training camps from which militants feed insurgencies in neighbouring countries. That such attacks go well beyond "hot pursuit", which American forces were doing anyway, is clear. Nevertheless, it is difficult to see how else to pacify Afghanistan: there is no doubt now that much of the insurgency in Afghanistan is fuelled from secure bases in the tribal areas; no counterinsurgency action in history has been successful without a sealed border; and the Pakistan army has shown itself unwilling to extend the rule of law all the way to its own frontier. Indeed, it appears that the army chief, General Kayani, was aware of what elements under his command planned to do to the Indian embassy in Kabul. Thus the raids are, after all, aimed at doing little more than what the Pakistan army was supposed to, and has not.

However, the timing is problematic: for America to step up its attacks when a civilian president generally seen as pro-American has just assumed office seems odd. It gives the army an excuse to further separate itself from civilian control and impede the "civilianising" process further — already Kayani has forced the PPP's hand by taking a hawkish stand on American action and a Pakistani official told The New York Times that the raids are "stupid" in that they are based on outdated information. Hopefully, the Pentagon has been careful evaluating the risk of military action, and has taken into account fractures in the local leadership and the possibility of faulty intelligence.

Heading: Delta blues - Indian Express
Content:
Raj Thackeray is always desperate for provocation. So it was entirely to be expected that he would eagerly take offence to a Mumbai police officer's statement that the city is nobody's preserve. Joint Commissioner of Police K.L. Prasad was stating, if colourfully, the only reaction that law enforcement authorities could have to the kind of intimidation and disruption Thackeray's Maharashtra Navanirman Sena has unleashed on Mumbai. No, Thackeray's bully tactics of asking the cop to meet him on the street do not surprise. What surprises is how lonely that official voice of defiance is. Ever since Thackeray hit upon his violent insistence that all of Mumbai swear by Marathi and pledge their devotion to the state, the state government has absented itself in word and action. By this sustained abdication, the government has allowed a single bully to prosper and tarnish the city with xenophobia.

For Thackeray, the targeting of Prasad comes conveniently fast upon his "acceptance" of an apology from Amitabh Bachchan for wife Jaya's reference to her Uttar Pradesh connections. Bachchan alone can say what compelled him to articulate his affection for Mumbai in terms that Thackeray would construe as an apology, instead of as a counter-vision of Mumbai's traditional inclusiveness of identities and ideas. This may not be a full explanation for Bachchan's personal choices, but it is true that members of civil society are intimidated against making individual noises of defiance when the state refuses to take cognisance of the outright flouting of laws. Thackeray has menaced not just sundry film actors. He has disrupted small businesses and normal life, each time in a manner that violates the law of the land. And each time, he has done so to be allowed to roam free to voice yet again his contrived politics of identity.

The silence of Maharashtra's politicians conveys two things. One, that they are loath to counter Thackeray for fear of alienating a possibly chauvinistic vote. Two, that they are letting Thackeray ignite divisions in the hope that the vote will split up to their advantage. As for the Maharashtra government, whether it is acting upon these concerns is immaterial. Because ultimately it is failing to meet its administrative responsibilities.

Heading: Guns and gales - Indian Express
Content:
Now that the initial attempts at disaster relief are over, it is time to look at the management of flood basins. I must be one of the few people in India to have read the text of the original Ganges Flood Control Commission and Brahmaputra Flood Control Board Report, each running into hundreds of pages with annexures and maps. The Ganga studies, unlike the Brahmaputra ones, do not really strategise properly. The Brahmaputra Flood Control Board went through a chequered history at one stage with a large number of employees, who had little to do with flood control, absorbed thanks to political pressure; but when I was in the Planning Commission, we chose A.B. Mohile and he did a super job.

Mohile developed the Brahmaputra flood control strategy in the larger context of the river as part of the economy and ecology of the region. For example, he dealt with the communications linkages of the Brahmaputra within the Northeast and with adjoining countries, which had been sadly disturbed over time. With the efforts of Mani Shankar Aiyar and Jairam Ramesh, the concept of the Brahmaputra basin as a region which has links with the Mekong and can become the strong arm of India's strategic objectives to the east is being revived. We need to talk about the Brahmaputra-Mekong region, rather than the Ganga-Mekong region.

Apart from this larger concept, Mohile's long-term plans included decentralised water development for energy, tree-based agriculture and inland waterway communication. Also, Mohile knew that a river changes its course. Embankments by themselves are never the whole answer and he developed the concept of "training" the river. This means a lot of work on hydrology, on sedimentation and an eye to the larger facts which determine the strategy of river basin development. It is obvious that flood management will have to be thought of in this larger perspective, rather than as just big dams.

Any strategy must view drainage as a mirror image of the desired water flows — which raises questions of land use and of the power of local oligarchies. Study after study in India show that local water bodies are clogged because influential people encroach either on the water body itself or on the approaches to it. In towns and large villages in flood prone areas, urban authorities think nothing of clogging historical drainage systems which took care of rivers in flood and monsoon waters.

The vice-chancellor of the Bidhan Agricultural University, a distinguished son of the soil and a scientist, showed that if every pond or pukur in the delta of Bengal is deepened by three metres, say, with an employment guarantee scheme, then around 10 per cent of surplus rainfall would be absorbed in village water bodies. Since floods can invariably be followed by droughts, in the winter and summer seasons the stored water could be used for paddy and other high value crops.

Even if we begin the long haul of sensible management of river basins, including afforestation and soil management of the area from which the rivers originally rise, there would still remain the Himalayan problem of dealing with our neighbours. There is no point in saying that Bhutan is already out of being a least developed country, having developed two hydel projects in cooperation with India, or that there was an agreement on a large hydel project with Nepal. If it has to start all over again, we need the patience to do it. We also need the vision to show how our larger reform processes are relevant for inter-regional trade and resource flows. I agree with some visionary Nepali policy-makers that India must pay the long-run marginal cost of energy and water. But diplomats who insist on starting negotiations with the phrase "low cost of the hydel project" have to keep in mind that, at the same time, the country is negotiating for gas-based power or nuclear power. Interestingly, every time we send an energy sector manager to negotiate outcomes with his counterparts instead of a diplomat, he comes back with roughly agreed solutions. Someone who manages a power grid thinks of the price at which the power can sell in India. India should also set aside — as I argued in "Our Common Future" — a billion dollars out of its hundreds of billions of dollars of exchange reserves for sustainable development of water and energy projects in the poorest districts of the sub-continent. Dams will only be a small part of it. The bigger part will be to share experiences at the village and aquifer and watershed levels to move the triangles of poverty and misery to a future of prosperity.

The writer, a former Union minister, is chairman, Institute of Rural Management, Anand

express@expressindia.com

Heading: The printed page still matters - Indian Express
Content:
They are like Siamese twins, Gabbar Singh the villain and his gun. The gun-wielding Gabbar, a fugitive from justice, pacing up and down in his hideout, grinning disapproval at his sidekicks for being shamed by the duo that had the audacity to challenge him on his turf. Gabbar has become an icon. Not long ago, his bête noire, who went on to become Big B in Bollywood, had no qualms about donning the mantle of the malefactor as if the villain, the epitome of the gun culture, had ceased to be an anathema.

If only the gun had not been invented! For it takes numerous lives. The killing machine is so easy to come by. You land one as swimmingly as you buy a loaf of bread. You might say the gun does not shoot; it is the shooter that pulls the trigger. True. But to a criminal, on a killing spree, a gun comes handier than a knife and the destruction it unleashes is massive. A gun wielder has a unique edge over his unarmed victims, as we witness in every mayhem.

Anthony Grayling, the British author, aptly begins an essay on guns with a quotation from Tagore which says, "He has made his weapons his gods. When his weapons win, he is defeated himself." The United States is home to periodic but predictable hurricanes. It is also home to trigger-happy and unpredictable gunslingers. Predictability takes the sting out of the gale. But a springing gun trotter surprises you — with death or misery. He bursts into classrooms or pounces upon unsuspecting picnickers. With his face vanishing into a sadistic scowl, he empties his bullets into innocents and snuffs out lives. "See you soon. No luck next time," he seems to tell the horror-stricken survivors scampering for cover. One dreads the prospect of this gun culture finding its way to our shores. Or is it already here? Perish that thought.

Heading: DIABETES: THE VIA MEDIA? - Indian Express
Content:
The words are the same, but those of you holding a newspaper as you read this column are having a different experience than those of you reading it on a computer screen. Consumers are trading print for pixels, scattering the ad money spent to reach them across their ever-expanding digital marketplace for information and entertainment. Yet the printed word is not an endangered species.

There will be survivors because, despite the undeniable thrill and usefulness of instant information from a variety of sources all at once, often for free, there is something to be said for the allure of attractive, well-tended hard copy.

"It's an emotional connection. It's a passionate connection. People do like to hold it, feel it, touch it," said Jason Binn, chief executive and founder of Niche Media, which is adding property to the shrinking media landscape with the introduction next week of Michigan Avenue, a Chicago-centric magazine catering to well-to-do readers and the marketers that dote on them. For all the info you might get everywhere else, you may like the newspaper because you do the crossword puzzle with your coffee, or

because you can fold it under your arm as you get on the "L." Maybe it's because you can crumple it up when you're done. But in the perishability of daily news is the medium's vulnerability.

Magazines, some magazines at least, may be another matter. Newsmagazines have an even greater challenge than newspapers to endure and remain relevant. But the high-end glossies trading in content with a more advanced expiration date enjoy an advantage in that jewellery, fashion, car, real estate and vacation ads look better on their heavy paper stock. Why do you suppose The Wall Street Journal launched a lifestyle magazine on Saturday? "Print offers a completely unique environment that is going to sustain and grow and improve," said David Granger, editor of Esquire, which is looking beyond the 75th anniversary it's about to mark. "The print experience is unique and it's profound... [But] we're fighting for readers' time with every other entertainment."

Excerpted from a comment by Phil Rosenthal in 'Chicago Tribune'

Heading: IBS: What are the foods you should avoid - Indian Express
Content:
In the last 12 months, two new diabetes drugs have been introduced in India and another one is expected to hit the market soon. Do these drugs bring any hope or are they just "me-too" drugs out to exploit the lucrative markets of the diabetes capital of the world?

"These drugs have an entirely different method of functioning which the drugs available so far did not have. Hopefully, this is just the beginning," said Dr Anoop Misra, Head of Department of Diabetes and Metabolism, Fortis hospitals.

The first of the drugs to be launched in India was Byetta (exenatide injection) in April 2007. It helped improve blood sugar control in patients with Type 2 diabetes.

The injectable drug was followed by Januvia (sitagliptin) by Merck.

It was approved for the treatment of Type 2 diabetes in India in May 2008 and is already being seen as a commercial success. Its once-a-day dose and lack of major side effects have been the key selling points.

"It has shown fantastic results on patients. The cost is also reasonable. Plus it is an oral drug. The patients are quite satisfied with it," said Dr Surendra Kumar, Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Sir Gangaram Hospital.

By next month, another drug, Galvus (vildagliptin) by Novartis is expected to join the league.

THE MODUS OPERANDI

These drugs especially hold promise for the Type 2 diabetes patients — who constitute 95 per cent of the diabetic population in the country.

But how do they work?

In diabetes, the body does not produce enough insulin, which is why, in extreme cases, insulin injections are necessary. What the new drugs do is that instead of providing more insulin, they stimulate the insulin producing cells — so they in turn, produce the required amount of insulin.

The drugs, said Dr Misra, act on pancreas, increase the release of insulin and more importantly, help in the formation of new cells in pancreas.

This is done through GLP1— an enzyme responsible for maintaining the health of the insulin-producing cells. The GLP1 — which is produced naturally in the body — gets destroyed within a minute, but the new drug is a synthetic version of GLP1 and lasts as long as 12 hours, which helps in production of insulin.

ARE THE drugs SAFE?

Most in the medical fraternity agree that the drugs are fairly safe and have few side effects.

But there is a warning though.

"None of these drugs can replace the existing medicines but they are useful add-ons," said Dr Ambrish Mittal, Senior Consultant, Department of Endocrinology, Indraprastha Apollo hospitals, New Delhi. "They have not yet become the drug of first choice but the findings are exciting."

Dr Misra agrees. "These drugs can be added to the existing drugs and can supplement the previous treatment. They are fairly effective and safe, though they might cause weight loss or nausea in some cases," he said.

TYPE 2 DIABETES IN INDIA

In Type 2 diabetes, patients are non-insulin dependent and they can control the glucose in their blood by eating measured diet, taking regular exercise and oral medication.

Worldwide, millions of people have Type 2 diabetes and most find out about it much later. But if not diagnosed and treated in time, such people may develop serious complications.

One of the major causes of the "diabetes epidemic" in India is the "thrifty gene syndrome" among Indians.

According to the theory, our ancestors developed the "thrifty gene" as a survival mechanism. It was meant to help store fat to help tide over famines.

But now that people have enough to eat and little work, the gene has become a liability. It gets activated because of sedentary lifestyle, bad food habits and improper sleep and cause diabetes.

If not cured, diabetes leads to several complications including renal disorder which can lead to kidney failure, blood vessel damage in eyes leading to blindness, nerve damage in feet leading to amputation and heart disease leading to death.

WHAT LIES AHEAD

So what does it portend for the Indian market? The experts agree that the arrival of the new pills is good news.

"We have better choice of drugs and the sudden interest the pharmaceutical companies are showing in Indian markets will be giving us a better variety of choices," said Dr Mittal.

But even so, the patients, they maintain, should bank more on physical work, proper diet and an overall healthy lifestyle instead of hoping for miracle pills.

Heading: The doctor is in - Indian Express
Content:
As RxPress pointed out last week, there has been a significant rise in the number of people suffering from Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). While it requires a gastroenterologist to rule out any pathology, diet plays a crucial role in treating the symptoms. Some foods act as triggers for the symptoms — recurrent abdominal pain, gas, distention of stomach, frequent diarrhoea or constipation — others have a calming effect. Mostly, an individual diet plan for every patient may work best.

What are the foods that aggravate the symptoms of IBS? The good news is that the list of offending foods is not exhaustive. Anything high in fat, caffeine, carbonated beverages, alcohol and insoluble fiber can mean trouble. These categories of foods act either as irritants or as stimulants for the gastrointestinal tract, which is why they could induce a spasm in the tract. It is not necessary to go for a fat-free diet. It would be enough to avoid high fat dairy products -- cream, cheese and butter.

Fried foods and chocolates are best had in limited amounts. If you crave the taste of chocolates it is acceptable to use cocoa powder but the solid chocolates are best avoided. The red meats should be avoided but while meat is acceptable. Seafood is also on the list of acceptable foods.

Tea, coffee, sodas and alcohol should be taken in very moderate amounts. If you must have a cup, make sure that you do not do so on an empty stomach. Insoluble fiber is the category of fiber that spells trouble for the IBS afflicted. There tends to be a great deal of confusion regarding the two kinds of fiber available from foods.

Insoluble fiber is the one available from bran and raw foods and veggies (there are some exceptions). What could be more confusing is the fact that most insoluble fiber foods are actually healthy foods and ought to be included in the diet.

The way around it would be to peel, core, chop, and cook or puree such foods. Nuts and seeds could be made into a paste and added to breads or cereals. Such modifications would mollify the effect of the insoluble fiber. In effect, this means one would get to eat less of raw veggies and fruits. Also, one must make sure not to consume these at the beginning of a meal but towards the end.

Of course, it must not be construed that these foods will cause IBS to anyone who consumes them. Rather, those who suffer from IBS tend to have it due to their consumption of some of these foods.

Next week: Foods that can help alleviate IBS symptoms

Heading: After a two-month battle, the baby recovered - Indian Express
Content:
I am 16 years old and get frequent headaches. Can you tell me what is the cause and how can I prevent it?

— Sanchit Sinha

Dr A K Bali, Consultant, Internal Medicine, Moolchand Medcity, says: Headaches, like chest pain or dizziness, can have many causes. Basically, headaches are of two types: primary and secondary. Primary headaches are not associated with (caused by) other diseases. Examples of primary headaches are migraine, tension headaches and cluster headaches. Secondary headaches are caused by associated disease. The associated disease may be minor or serious and life-threatening. The common reasons of headaches include lack of sleep, oversleep, fasting for long on regular intervals, too much of stress and tension and intake of cholesterol-rich diet. It is advisable to get yourself examined. Nowadays many hospitals have dedicated headache clinics.

Does migraines occur in the afternoons? And what treatment is advisable? — Ritika Verma

Dr Bali says: Migraine is the second-most common type of primary headache. It affects children and adults. Before puberty, boys and girls are affected equally, but after puberty, more women than men are affected. Migraine is usually accompanied by nausea, facial pallor, cold hands, cold feet and sensitivity to light and sound and smell of perfumes. As a result of this sensitivity to light and sound, migraine sufferers usually prefer a quiet, dark room during an attack. A typical attack lasts between 4 and 72 hours. Usually, the best treatment is to avoid the trigger factors like lack of sleep, oversleeping, fasting for long hours, exposure to sun, tension, stress, and fast foods like chocolates.

Heading: The tears just keep coming - Indian Express
Content:
It was a winter night ten years ago, when my hospital rang up. It was freezing outside. Still, after hearing what they had to say, I was dressed and out in a flash. Random thoughts ran through my mind as I tried to prepare myself for the long vigil in the Intensive Care Unit that lay ahead.

It was nevertheless a shock to see this newborn gasping for air, in severe respiratory distress, with a very low pulse and blood pressure.

The laboratory tests and initial X-rays held out little hope. The baby had severe bronchopneumonia, massive plural effusions (collection of fluids in both lungs), ascites (fluid in the abdominal cavity), electrolyte disturbances, life threatening infection, abnormal functioning of liver and acute failure of the kidneys. The child was almost in shock.

After a quick assessment, I spoke to the family waiting outside the neo-natal ICU. The parents had given up all hope. And the situation had to be explained to them.

What was required was urgent intervention? The baby needed to be put on life support systems like ventilation, invasive monitoring, peritoneal dialysis for renal failure and medications for pneumonia and low blood pressure. Problem was, these procedures on sick newborns are not only technically difficult but it is early diagnosis and management which can save them.

Unfortunately for us, the baby had been shifted to us from another hospital three days after birth, when the complications had set in. The battle to save its life which began that night, was to last over two months.

The parents, under severe mental pressure, just prayed. The image of them waiting outside the ICU for hours every day is clearly etched in my mind.

After such a prolonged hospital stay, we tend to develop an emotional attachment with the child and the family. So it was a happy day for me too, when the baby recovered against all odds. The morning the child was discharged, the gratitude of the parents brought tears to my eyes.

For me, the experience reinstated my faith in perseverance and hard work. But the joy of the parents — in having their baby restored to health and watching him grow over the years - is my biggest reward.

Heading: Sarah Hawk ready to swoop on Russia (perhaps), and Pak - Indian Express
Content:
Under chill gray clouds that gradually gave way to patches of blue, New York City paused on Thursday to observe the seventh anniversary of a day that Mayor Michael R Bloomberg said "began like any other and ended like no other".

Tearful and often defiant, and waving large photos of some of the 2,751 people killed at the World Trade Center, hundreds of relatives and friends steeled themselves and marked the passing of another year since terrorists crashed two hijacked jets into the twin towers. Others gathered in smaller remembrances around the region, in firehouses and parks and houses of worship.

For the second year, construction kept the main ceremony out of the excavated hole at ground zero, but many mourners bearing bouquets were escorted down a ramp to the towers' footprints. A few hours later, both major presidential candidates made the same trek into the pit.

The name of every victim was read aloud and announced by 105 pairs of readers. Each pair included a relative of a victim and a foreign student representing one of the 95 countries that lost someone in the carnage. It took more than three hours to intone all the names.

A bell chimed and the crowd fell silent at four moments: 8.46 am, when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the north tower; 9.03, when United Flight 175 hit the south tower; 9.59, when the south tower collapsed; and 10.29, when the north tower fell.

The reading of some names was accompanied by the release of heart-shaped balloons that drifted over the crowd and out of sight northward over the downtown skyline. When they came to their own son, daughter, husband or wife, many readers added a poignant personal note. "Mommy and I wish you a happy birthday," said one father.

The service opened with the display of the torn American flag that had flown over the World Trade Center and included brief inspirational readings by Governors David A Paterson of New York and Jon S Corzine of New Jersey, former mayor Rudolph W Giuliani, former Governor George E Pataki, and Michael Chertoff, the secretary of homeland security.

Along Broadway, thousands of onlookers strained against police barricades to catch a glimpse of the ceremony unfolding against a backdrop of construction cranes. One young woman in a white dress shirt and pearls stopped to observe the moment of silence amid the bustle. She closed her eyes, nodded her head and began to sway ever so slightly from side to side. And when the bells stopped, she opened her eyes to let tears stream down her cheeks.

A male hand reached out to squeeze her shoulder, and she leaned into her companion, wiping the tears away.

As in the city on September 11, 2001, and in the days after, grief mixed with polarized political opinions.

About four dozen people protested near Church and Vesey streets wearing black T-shirts emblazoned with slogans like "Investigate 9/11 — honour the fallen with the relentless pursuit of truth" and "9/11 was an inside job". At a small plaza near Liberty Street, a shouting match broke out about terrorism and politics, but the police quickly broke it up.

Around 4 pm, the two major presidential nominees, Senators John McCain and Barack Obama, walked together down the ramp, with McCain's wife, Cindy, and Mayor Bloomberg behind them. Michelle Obama was home in Chicago with the couple's daughters.

At firehouses around the city, the day was marked with solemnity. At Engine 4 and Ladder 15 on South Street, firefighters in navy blue dress uniforms lined up in rows to observe the moments the two planes struck and the towers crumbled. The two companies lost 14 members on September 11, 2001.

At 8.46 in Park Slope, 24 firefighters from Engine Company 220, Engine Company 239 and Ladder Company 122 stood in dress uniforms outside their side-by-side firehouses on 11th Street. The flag was at half-staff. A buzzer went off. A voice on a loudspeaker said, "We will now observe a moment of silence for all members of the department who gave their lives on September 11, 2001."

United in grief, BUT a DAY later, back to the big fight

John McCain and Barack Obama (above) visited Ground Zero in New York to remember and mourn the 9/11 tragedy. As soon as the day passed, however, the attacks at each other returned. Obama was first off the blocks on Friday, his campaign releasing a TV ad that mocked Mccain as an out-of-touch, out-of-date computer illiterate.

Obama's new, vicious fighting spirit comes as McCain gains in the polls, with some Democrats expressing concern that the Obama campaign has not been aggressive enough. The campaign says the escalation will involve advertising and pushes by both Obama and Joe Biden.

Heading: Palin says she’s a proud ‘hockey mom’. So what’s the hockey way of life in Alaska? - Indian Express
Content:
Sarah Palin presented the face of a foreign policy hawk in her first interview since becoming Republican John McCain's running mate, taking a hard line on Iran and Pakistan, and saying the U S should "perhaps" go to war with Russia on the issue of Georgia.

She also reversed her stand on the cause of climate change, telling ABC News anchor Charles Gibson that she believes "man's activities certainly can be contributing to the issue of global warming." Less than a year ago, she had said the opposite.

By turns tense and combative, Palin, 44, used two interviews with Gibson to display her grasp of issues central to the vice presidency, chief among them foreign policy, where she has been portrayed as a novice in comparison to her Democratic rival, wonk Joe Biden.

She acknowledged that, other than a trip last year to see troops in Iraq, Kuwait and Germany, her only visits abroad were to Mexico and Canada. And she said that she had never met a head of state but that she did speak last week with President Mikhail Saakashvili of Georgia.

Palin called the Russian incursion into Georgia last month "unprovoked," a view at odds with that of Bush administration officials who have reviewed events leading up to the military action.

She said she favoured bringing Ukraine and Georgia into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), even though Russia would consider such a move a threat to its security. And when Gibson asked whether she would then have the U S go to war in response to a Russian invasion of Georgia, she said: "Perhaps so. I mean, that is the agreement when you are a NATO ally, is if another country is attacked, you're going to be expected to be called upon and help."

On Iran, Palin said nuclear weapons under the control of President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad would be "extremely dangerous to everyone on this globe". She called for a hands-off approach to Israel if it decided to strike Iranian nuclear facilities. "We cannot second-guess the steps that Israel has to take to defend itself."

Palin stumbled somewhat when Gibson asked her if she agreed with the Bush Doctrine, which holds that the U S can wage preemptive war against hostile nations. She then said: "I believe that what President Bush has attempted to do is rid this world of Islamic extremism, terrorists who are hellbent on destroying our nation," adding, "There have been blunders along the way, though. There have been mistakes made."

Pressed repeatedly on whether the U S could attack terrorist hideouts in Pakistan without Islamabad's permission, she said: "If there is legitimate and enough intelligence that tells us that a strike is imminent against American people, we have every right to defend our country. In fact, the president has the obligation, the duty to defend."

On the question of whether she was ready to step in as president if needed, Palin said she was. She also said she had not hesitated to accept McCain's offer to join the ticket.

Are we just supposed to wipe bloody snot and hang our heads: Putin

MOSCOW: Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin aggressively defended the invasion of Georgia before a group of Western journalists on Thursday, asking them: "Are we supposed to just wipe away bloody snot and hang our heads?" Rejecting Western allegations that Moscow used excessive force, Putin said: "When tanks, multiple rocket launchers and heavy artillery are used against us (by Georgia's U S-trained army), are we supposed to fire with slingshots?

Heading: Another US strike kills 12, PML(N) wants House session - Indian Express
Content:
Like many parents here in the communities near Anchorage, Sarah Palin raised her older children in (ice) hockey rinks.

Powered on white mochas and an aerobics class or two, Palin would drive to rinks at all hours, children in tow. She sometimes ran the scoreboard, let hockey players from other cities sleep on the floor of her home and got involved in the management of her eldest son's teams.

Although hockey players enjoy a reputation as rowdy partiers at many high schools, the sport often keeps children here on the straight and narrow, much the way football and basketball do in other places. When Dan Johnston — second cousin to 18-year-old Levi Johnston, the would-be father of Palin's daughter Bristol's child — sold raffle tickets for his son's team, his sales slogan was, "Help keep the kids on the ice and off the streets."

But hockey can also be a roiling pressure cooker, full of big expectations and bigger disappointments, especially across south-central Alaska where it is highly competitive and many parents harbour hopes that their children might get a college scholarship and maybe even make it to the National Hockey League.

If football dominates Friday nights in rural Texas, hockey dominates here.

"All of us basically raise our kids here from August to March," said Donna Cooley, who has an out-of-town Avalanche team player as a boarder and a 12-year-old son who plays. "We call the kids 'rink rats,' and we all miss each other when the season ends."

To understand hockey in Alaska is to understand something about the Palin family dynamic: Athletic drive seems to be as much a family trait as churchgoing and salmon fishing.

Palin's father was a popular cross-country coach. She was a high school basketball star who married Todd Palin, a high school jock who has remained an athlete as an adult. Mr Palin is a four-time winner of the Iron Dog snowmobile race, something akin to Nascar elsewhere in terms of its local celebrity.

Wasilla's four-year-old sports complex, where the Avalanche and other teams play, is a $15 million legacy from the days when Palin was mayor. And even before Track, her eldest son, was in elementary school, his parents had him on skates.

In more rural parts of the state, where gyms instead of hockey rinks were built with the rush of oil money in the 1980s, basketball is the favoured sport. But in and around Anchorage, particularly in wealthier high schools, hockey is everything.

With $400 skates, $150 sticks and hundreds of dollars more for pads and gloves, outfitting a skater can cost well over $1,000. Add in ice time, league fees and the cost of travel in and out of this state, and some families with elite high school players can spend $15,000 a year.

Parents with especially talented skaters or with enough money or both often do what the Palins eventually did with Track Palin: Write a check and send him to hockey development programs out of state.

Heading: Power-sharing deal in Zimbabwe - Indian Express
Content:
A day after Pakistan's army chief lashed out at U S raids inside Pakistani territory, the party of former prime minister Nawaz Sharif called for parliament to meet in joint session to devise strategy on how to deal with the cross-border attacks. The call came after a latest suspected U S missile strike killed 12 people in northwestern Pakistan before dawn on Friday.

US forces in Afghanistan are stepping up their efforts to hit Taliban and al-Qaida militants in what they call safe havens in Pakistan's wild border regions, despite stiff protests from Islamabad.

With the insurgency in Afghanistan intensifying, President George W Bush has been reported to have secretly approved more aggressive cross-border operations in July.

Chaudhry Nisar Ali, senior PML (Nawaz) leader, on Friday demanded the government convene a joint session of parliament to discuss and devise a strategy on what he called an increasing and alarming number of U S strikes inside Pakistan. "This is very serious and very concerning to us," he said.

According to Pakistani intelligence officials, missiles struck a home near Miran Shah, the main town in the North Waziristan tribal region, before dawn on Friday, killing 12 people and injuring 10. Since August 20, there have been at least seven reported missile strikes as well as a raid by helicopter-borne U S commandos that Pakistani officials claim killed 15 people, all civilians. Both the U S military and the CIA operate unmanned drone aircraft armed with missiles of the type believed to have killed two senior al-Qaida commanders in Pakistani territory earlier this year.

Army chief General Ashfaq Pervez Kayani, in a strongly worded statement on Thursday, accused the U S of "reckless action" that violated international rules of engagement, and vowed to defend the "territorial integrity and sovereignty" of Pakistan "at all cost".

On Friday, army spokesman Major Murad Khan said 32 militants and 2 soldiers had died in Pakistani armed forces action in the previous 24 hours in the Bajur region.

Heading: To slow global warming, install white roofs - Indian Express
Content:
President Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe and the Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai struck a power-sharing deal on Thursday after more than a month of wrangling, but it was still far from clear how the bitter foes would divide the authority to govern.

The agreement, brokered by President Thabo Mbeki of South Africa, signals that Mugabe may be willing to cede some authority to Tsvangirai, loosening the tight grip on power he has maintained for nearly three decades and easing the political crisis that has engulfed Zimbabwe for months.

They did not spell out how the deal would work, but Mbeki said the details of the agreement would be released on Monday at a signing ceremony. Officials in both the governing and opposition parties described an arrangement that seemed to leave neither man clearly in charge. That may reduce the chances that the accord will bring stability and attract the foreign aid needed to rebuild the country's ruined economy.

Under the agreement, officials said, Tsvangirai would become PM and oversee a council of ministers that would formulate and carry out policies. Mugabe would retain his title of president and would lead a cabinet of the ministers that would supervise the council. That arrangement appears to give both men the power to oversee the same group of ministers.

Asked who would lead the government, Nelson Chamisa, a spokesman for the opposition Movement for Democratic Change, did not name one man or the other, but instead replied, "this is an inclusive government." He said executive power would be shared by the president, the prime minister and the cabinet.

Zimbabwe has faced political stalemate since Mugabe, 84, held onto the presidency in a June runoff that was widely denounced as a sham.

Heading: Crackdown on Pro-Tibet activists in Nepal - Indian Express
Content:
Builders have known for decades that white roofs reflect the sun's rays and lower the cost of air conditioning. But now scientists say they have quantified a new benefit: slowing global warming.

If the 100 biggest cities in the world installed white roofs and changed their pavements to more reflective materials — say, concrete instead of asphalt — the global cooling effect would be massive, according to data released this week at California's annual Climate Change Research Conference in Sacramento.

Since 2005, California has required that flat commercial structures have white roofs. Next year, new and retrofitted residential and commercial buildings, with both flat and sloped roofs, will have to install heat-reflecting roofing, as part of an energy-efficient building code. But the state has not yet passed any rules to encourage cooler pavements and roads.

According to Hashem Akbari, a physicist with the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, a 1,000-square-foot roof — the average size on an American home — offsets 10 metric tons of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions in the atmosphere if dark-colored shingles or coatings are replaced with white material.
